title: Set a pointer to 120 degrees on a graduated dial
instruction: Lay the blue pointer flat across the centre of the dial, lined up with the 120 degree graduation. The red tick is zero and the scale runs to 180 degrees.
context: During integration a technician clocks loose parts, such as a sensor bracket or an alignment bar, to a commanded angle on a fixed degree dial used as a layout template. The angle comes from a drawing, not from a mark painted at the answer. This 1 g tabletop analogue keeps that: the dial has no numerals, only a red zero tick, long ticks at 90 and 180 and short ticks every 15 degrees, and the 120 tick looks like every other short tick. The policy must find zero and the direction the scale runs, then count to 120, two short ticks past the 90 tick. Knob and ruler tasks turn or pull to a mark that stands out; here the target looks like its neighbours. The pointer starts parallel to the 90 degree line, so carrying it across without turning it scores 0, and so do 105 and 135, one tick off. Reading analogue scales is routine bench work and a known weak point of vision-language models. Earth gravity on a bench, where this job is done; no microgravity is claimed.
setup: Station table, in front of the left arm; the right arm is idle at its ready pose. Table coordinates in metres: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y left from the midline, heights above the table top; the left arm's base is at y = +0.305. All objects are rigid and matte with one shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic). Fixed: the dial, a white (sRGB 0.92, 0.92, 0.90) disc 240 mm across and 6 mm tall, centred at (0.230, 0.305), spanning x 0.110 to 0.350 and y 0.185 to 0.425. Dial angles run from the centre: 0 toward +y (the robot's left), 90 toward +x (straight ahead), 180 toward -y (toward the midline); angle a points along (sin a, cos a). On the dial top, 0.5 mm proud, thirteen graduations every 15 degrees from 0 to 180 over the far half, each an 8 mm wide strip running along its angle's ray, with no numerals. The short ones (15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 105, 120, 135, 150, 165) are black (sRGB 0.05, 0.05, 0.05) and run from radius 93 to 118 mm. The long ones at 90 and 180 are black and run from radius 78 to 118 mm; the long one at 0 is red (sRGB 0.85, 0.12, 0.12). So the 0 tick spans y 0.383 to 0.423 at x 0.230, the 90 tick x 0.308 to 0.348 at y 0.305, the 180 tick y 0.187 to 0.227 at x 0.230, and the 120 tick is centred at (0.321, 0.252). A black (sRGB 0.05, 0.05, 0.05) centre cross, two strips 24 x 4 mm and 0.5 mm proud, along x and along y, marks the centre. Loose: the pointer, a blue (sRGB 0.15, 0.40, 0.85) bar 170 x 24 x 20 mm, 80 g, lying flat on a 170 x 24 face with its long axis along x, centred at (0.200, 0.110), between the dial and the midline, 63 mm clear of the dial edge and 0.279 m from the left arm's base. It starts parallel to the 90 degree line. Nominal end state: the bar on the centre cross with its long axis at world yaw -30 degrees (30 degrees clockwise seen from above), along (0.866, -0.500); its ends then sit at radius 85 mm, 8 mm inside the short ticks, so it points at the 120 graduation without covering it. To build it: cut a 240 mm disc from 6 mm white acrylic or MDF and tape it to the table at the stated centre; mark the graduations with 8 mm black and red vinyl tape cut to length, laid out with a protractor from the zero ray; cut the bar from hardwood or print it in PLA, weight it to 80 g and paint it blue; tape a mark for its start spot.
scoring: End state only, judged after the arm has released and moved clear, from a top photo, a protractor and a tape; in simulation on the final step (SCORE_OVER end) from the bar's centre and quaternion, not its axis-aligned bounds. The pointer is placed when it is at rest (under 10 mm/s and 0.5 rad/s), its long axis is within 5 degrees of level (any of its four long faces may be down), its lowest point is within 3 mm of the dial top (on the centre cross it is 0.5 mm up) and its centre is within 12 mm of the dial centre (0.230, 0.305). Two angles are then read, each folded because the bar is symmetric end for end, so either end may point at 120. The axis error e is the angle between the bar's long axis, seen from above, and the 120 degree ray. The scale error s is the angle about the dial centre between the 120 tick and the point where the bar's centre line, extended, crosses the tick ring (radius 105.5 mm, the middle of the short ticks): where the bar points on the scale, so a bar shifted sideways onto another graduation fails. Placed with e and s both at most 5 degrees: 1.0, the success condition, which ends the trial once it has held for 1 s. Placed otherwise with both under 7.5 degrees: 0.5, the right graduation read but set loosely; the bar and the point it reads are both still nearer 120 than 105 or 135. Anything else: 0, including a bar placed on any other graduation, off centre by more than 12 mm, tilted along its length, still moving, held more than 3 mm up, on the table or partly off the dial. Reference outcomes, centred: on the 90 tick, as it starts, e = 30, so 0; on 105 or 135, one graduation off, 0; on 60, the scale read from the 180 end, 0; on zero, 0; at 113 or 127, 0.5; at 112.5, midway, 0; at 115 or 125, 1.0; upside down, reversed or on a 170 x 20 face at 120, 1.0. Off centre with the axis on 120: 11.9 mm along the bar, 1.0; 11.9 mm sideways, s = 6.5, so 0.5. At 115.1 and 11.9 mm sideways toward 105, s = 11.4, so 0. With a tape: e is within 5 (7.5) degrees when the centres of the bar's two end faces, measured square to the line from the dial centre through the 120 tick, differ in offset by at most 14.8 (22.2) mm; s is within 5 (7.5) degrees when the extended centre line meets the tick ring within 9.2 (13.8) mm of the 120 tick's middle. The start state scores 0. Pushing the bar at the 6 mm dial edge stops it or tips it, and it would still have to end centred and at the right angle; a bar dropped or knocked from elsewhere does not come to rest centred on 120 by chance. A value exactly on a limit passes (0.1 mm and 0.001 degree margins), except 7.5 degrees, which is equidistant from two graduations and scores 0. The dial cannot move in simulation; on the real rig a trial in which it moves more than 5 mm from its mark scores 0. In simulation release is inferred from the bar being at rest, so a bar held perfectly still would also count; on real arms the photo after the gripper opens and withdraws decides.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Lay the pointer back flat on its mark with its long axis forward; the dial and its graduations do not move.
fidelity: Approximate: rigid primitives with one shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic) and matte colours; the dial cannot move. A real part is often clocked about its own pin or bolt circle; here a plain bar is laid free across a fixed dial, which keeps the reading and the set angle and drops the pivot. Real dials are numbered; these 0.5 mm proud strips carry none, since numerals that fit this dial would be about 2 px tall at 320 x 176. Earth gravity on a bench, where this job is done.
